STAT 451 · Group Project

Which Measurements
Diagnose a Breast Mass?

Working out which of 30 nuclear measurements actually matter

Amoolya · Bonnie · Dhruvika · Kalynn · Edward

Breast Cancer Wisconsin (Diagnostic) · 569 masses · UCI ML Repository

Amoolya

The question

Our question and our data

  • In a fine-needle breast biopsy, the sample is photographed and software measures the cell nuclei.
  • 569 masses, 37% malignant. Ten measurements, each reported three ways (mean, standard error, and a “worst” value), so 30 features.
  • Which measurements actually separate malignant from benign, and how few do you need?

We split the data once, 80/20 and stratified. Everything after that (model, hyperparameters, feature ranking, cutoff) came from 5-fold cross-validation on the 455 training masses. We left the 114 test masses alone until the end.

Amoolya

What the data shows

Size and shape do most of the work

Edward

A problem

The features repeat each other

21 of the 435 pairs correlate above 0.90. Radius, perimeter and area are the same measurement three times over (r = 0.998).

Edward

Why it matters

So we did not trust the coefficients

We refit LASSO on 200 bootstrap resamples. Some size feature is kept every time, but which one is close to random. If we had just read one fitted model, we would have picked whichever it happened to keep.

Bonnie

Model comparison

Which model should we use?

All tuned by cross-validation on the training set. SVM (RBF) (C = 10, gamma = 0.01) wins by 0.0004 AUC over SVM (linear), which is not a difference a patient would notice. The decision tree is the one that lags (0.962): its splits are axis-aligned while the two groups separate along a diagonal, and a single tree varies a lot from fold to fold.

Bonnie

Model comparison

…and it barely mattered

  • Best to worst is 0.034 AUC across seven tuned models, and nearly all of it is the decision tree: the other six sit within 0.005 of each other.
  • We ranked models by AUC, which does not depend on where you put the cutoff, and then chose the cutoff separately on the cost of a missed cancer.

If the algorithm is not the story, the variables are. So that is where we spent the rest of our time.

Dhruvika

Cutting it down

How many features do we actually need?

Six named measurements (worst perimeter, mean concavity, se area, worst compactness, se concave pts and worst texture) reach 0.991 AUC against 0.995 for all 30. Principal components (uncorrelated axes sorted by how much variance they explain) do slightly better, but by at most 0.009 AUC. You also need 10 of them for 95% of the variance, and none is something a pathologist could measure.

Dhruvika

A surprise

One result we did not expect

  • worst texture is kept in 100% of resamples and comes first on out-of-fold permutation importance.
  • But on its own it ranks only 17th of 30 (AUC 0.79).
  • We think that is because it is almost uncorrelated with size (r = 0.37).

What matters is whether a feature adds something new, not how strong it looks on its own.

Kalynn

Two features at once

Putting two measurements together

Worst radius and worst smoothness, r = 0.22, cross-validated AUC 0.983 for the RBF-SVM drawn here. It is the best pair of a search, so treat that AUC as a ceiling. A big nucleus is malignant whatever its smoothness. Smoothness only changes the answer for mid-sized ones.

Kalynn

Choosing the cutoff

Missing a cancer is worse than a false alarm

So we set the cutoff for 98% sensitivity in training cross-validation instead of going for the best accuracy. On the test set we caught 42 of 42 malignant masses, at 94.4% specificity and 96.5% accuracy, against 62.7% for guessing benign every time. The six named features caught all 42 too, at 90.3% specificity. Training AUC 0.998 vs test 0.999, so it does not look overfit. Both models were fixed before we opened the test set, and we scored them in one pass.

All five

Conclusion

What we found

  • Malignant nuclei are bigger, more deeply indented and more unevenly textured.
  • A measurement’s worst reading beats its average (0.86 vs 0.83 average AUC).
  • Six measurements do about as well as thirty (0.991 vs 0.995 AUC): worst perimeter, mean concavity, se area, worst compactness, se concave pts and worst texture.
  • Weaknesses: one lab, early 1990s, hand-picked and human-segmented samples. Only 114 test cases, so specificity is good to about ±5 points.

Where you set the cutoff is really a medical decision, not a statistical one.
